cards.q: Root of an E-shape barre is on which string?
A-shape barre at fret 3 is which chord?

steps: **E-shape barre:** root on the 6th string. F at fret 1, G at fret 3, A at fret 5.
**A-shape barre:** root on the 5th string. B at fret 2, C at fret 3, D at fret 5.
For minor, use the Em or Am shape barred.
Your Bm/B shapes: index barre at fret 2, ring/little finger on frets 4.
For a clean F, place one finger at a time, starting with the corner (index barre).
barre-chords.summary: E-shape on the 6th string, A-shape on the 5th.
barre-chords.title: Barre and movable chords

cards.q: How many beats in a bar of 4/4?
How do you count beats divided in two?

cards.a: Play on 1 and let it ring through 2

steps: **4 beats = 1 bar.** Count 1 2 3 4 with the metronome and strum once per beat.
**Combining beats:** let one note ring across two beats. Play on 1, hold through 2, then play on 3 and 4. Try ringing 2→3, then 3→4, then 4→1 of the next bar.
**Dividing the beat:** split each beat in two: 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 &. Downstrum on the numbers, upstrum on the &s.
Mix them: e.g. beat 1 held through 2, then 3 & 4 &. Practise this over C major and A minor.
beats-bars.summary: Four beats make a bar; combine and divide them.
beats-bars.title: Beats and bars

cards.q: Which note turns minor pentatonic into blues?

cards.a: A C D E♭ E G

steps: Add the **♭5** to minor pentatonic: A blues = A C D **E♭** E G.
The blue note is a passing note. Slide or bend through it, don't sit on it.
You hear it all over Mary Had a Little Lamb, Still Got the Blues and Cocaine.
blues-scale.title: The blues scale

cards.a: So the solo sounds connected to the harmony
cards.q: Why target chord tones at chord changes?

steps: G major chord notes around frets 7–10: 5S10F G, 4S9F B, 3S7F D, 2S8F G, 1S7F B, 1S10F D.
E minor chord notes around frets 4–8: 6S7F B, 5S7F E, 4S5F G, 3S4F B, 2S5F E, 2S8F G, 1S7F B.
Improvise across all strings until the chord changes. When it changes, jump to the top 3 strings and hit a chord note.
Landing on a chord note at the change is what makes a solo sound like it follows the song.
chord-tones.summary: Know where each chord's notes sit in your scale position.
chord-tones.title: Targeting chord tones

cards.q: How many frets is a whole step?
Which natural notes have no sharp between them?
What note is one fret above B?

exercises.how: Index on fret 5, one finger per fret.
exercises.title: A chromatic at the 5th fret

steps: There are **12 notes**. Starting from E: E F F♯ G G♯ A A♯ B C C♯ D D♯, then E again an octave higher.
One fret = a **half step**. Two frets = a **whole step**.
**E→F** and **B→C** are only one fret apart. Every other pair of neighbouring letters has a sharp/flat between them.
Going **up** we usually name the in-between notes with sharps (♯). Going **down**, with flats (♭). F♯ and G♭ are the same fret.

Your teacher's G and A chromatic exercises: start at the 3rd fret (G) or 5th fret (A) on the 6th string and play every fret across the strings. Shift up one fret when you move from the 3rd string to the 2nd.
chromatic.summary: Half steps, whole steps and the two natural half steps.
chromatic.title: The 12 notes, sharps and flats

cards.q: What makes a chord a dominant 7th?

cards.a: A minor with G in the bass

steps: **Dominant 7th (B7, A7, E7):** major chord + minor 7th. Bluesy, pulls to the next chord. Used in Dancing Queen, Mary Had a Little Lamb.
**Major 7th (Fmaj7, Cmaj7):** major chord + major 7th. Soft and dreamy. Let It Be, Can't Stop, Still Got the Blues.
**Sus chords (Esus4, Dsus2):** replace the 3rd with the 4th or 2nd. Open and unresolved. There She Goes, Gently Weeps.
**E7♯9:** the Hendrix chord. Major 3rd and a sharp 9th clash on purpose. Mary Had a Little Lamb.
**Slash chords (Am/G):** chord over a different bass note. Gently Weeps walks the bass down Am → Am/G → F♯m7♭5 → Fmaj7.
**Half-diminished (F♯m7♭5):** diminished triad + minor 7th.
extended-chords.summary: B7, E7♯9, Esus4, Dsus2, Am/G, Fmaj7, F♯m7♭5.
extended-chords.title: 7ths, sus and slash chords in songs

cards.a: One scale note on beat 1 of every bar

cards.q: Over a C major track, which chord's notes for bar 4?

steps: Bookmark a C major or A minor backing track. Use strings 1–4.
1) On beat 1 of each bar, play one note from the scale.
2) Play a note on beats 1 and 3. Try random orders.
3) Pick notes that sound good with the chord. Avoid ones that clash.
4) Play a different note on all 4 beats, at 0.75 speed.
5) Add combining beats. 6) Add dividing beats. 7) Mix combining, dividing and normal beats.
8) On the 4th bar of each phrase, play notes from the G major chord (C major key) or E minor chord (A minor key).
improv-steps.summary: Nine steps, from one note per bar to full phrases.
improv-steps.title: Improvising over a backing track

cards.q: How many frets is a perfect 5th?
4 frets from the root is a…
3 frets from the root is a…

exercises.how: Root, major 3rd, root, minor 3rd, root, 5th, root, octave. Hum each pair.
exercises.title: Root to 3rd, 5th and octave on the A string

intervals.fix: Your Sep 2022 interval list says “root → 4 frets = major 2nd”. 4 frets is a major 3rd. A major 2nd is 2 frets.
steps: An **interval** is the distance between two notes. The first note is the **root**, the second is the **interval note**.

Count frets from the root:
1 fret = minor 2nd · 2 = major 2nd
3 = minor 3rd · 4 = major 3rd
5 = perfect 4th · 6 = diminished 5th
7 = perfect 5th · 8 = minor 6th
9 = major 6th · 10 = minor 7th
11 = major 7th · 12 = octave
**Hum it.** Play the root, then the interval note, and hum both. This is practising intervals by humming. It trains your ear to hear them.
The 3rd decides major or minor (4 frets = major, 3 = minor). The 5th (7 frets) sounds stable and is the other note in a power chord.
intervals.summary: Count frets from the root to name any interval.
intervals.title: Intervals: the distance between two notes

cards.a: C Dm Em F G Am B°
G Am Bm C D Em F♯°

cards.q: The vi chord in G major?

cards.a: I ii iii IV V vi vii°
cards.q: Roman numerals in a major key?

key-chords.fix: Your F major key page writes the 4th chord as A♯ major. In F major it's spelled B♭ (each letter once): F G A B♭ C D E.
steps: From each scale note, take every other note (1-3-5) to build a chord.
**C major key:** C · Dm · Em · F · G · Am · B° (I ii iii IV V vi vii°).
**G major key:** G · Am · Bm · C · D · Em · F♯°.
**F major key:** F · Gm · Am · B♭ · C · Dm · E°.
**A minor key:** Am · B° · C · Dm · Em · F · G (i ii° III iv v VI VII).
Major keys have mostly major chords in I, IV, V; minor keys mostly minor in i, iv, v.
key-chords.summary: Stack every other note of the scale.
key-chords.title: The 7 chords in a key

cards.a: F C G D A E B
B E A D G C F

steps: **Order of sharps:** F C G D A E B. A key with 2 sharps always has F♯ and C♯.
**Order of flats:** B E A D G C F. A key with 4 flats (A♭ major) has B♭ E♭ A♭ D♭.
Going up a 5th adds a sharp: C (0) → G (1) → D (2) → A (3) → E (4) → B (5).
Going up a 4th adds a flat: C (0) → F (1) → B♭ (2) → E♭ (3) → A♭ (4) → D♭ (5).
key-signatures.summary: Why sharps and flats come in a fixed order.
key-signatures.title: Key signatures and the circle of fifths

steps: Formula: **root + major 3rd (4 frets) + perfect 5th (3 more frets)**.
**C** = C E G · **F** = F A C · **G** = G B D.
Find them on the neck: C on the 5th string 3rd fret, E on the 4th string 2nd fret, G on the open 3rd string. That's your open C chord.
Open chords just repeat those three notes across more strings.
major-chord.title: Building a major chord

cards.q: Which notes are removed for major pentatonic?

steps: Take the major scale and drop the **4th and 7th**: C major pentatonic = **C D E G A**.
Five notes, no half steps, so nothing clashes. That's why it's easy to improvise with.
C major pentatonic and A minor pentatonic use the same five notes.
major-pent.summary: The major scale without its 4th and 7th.
major-pent.title: Major pentatonic

cards.a: W W H W W W H
C D E F G A B

cards.q: Which steps are half steps in a major scale?

exercises.how: From low E up and back. Start slow.
exercises.title: C major, open position

steps: A major scale picks **7 of the 12 notes**. From the root: whole, whole, half, whole, whole, whole, half (**W W H W W W H**).
As intervals: root, major 2nd, major 3rd, perfect 4th, perfect 5th, major 6th, major 7th, octave.
Start on C and it lands only on natural notes: **C D E F G A B C**.
Play it along **one string** first (e.g. the 5th string from C at fret 3) so you can see the gaps. Then play it in open position.
major-scale.summary: W W H W W W H: seven of the twelve notes.
major-scale.title: The major scale

steps: **Minor:** root + **minor 3rd (3 frets)** + perfect 5th (4 more). A minor = A C E · D minor = D F A · E minor = E G B.
On an open chord, lowering the 3rd by one fret turns major into minor: A → Am, E → Em.
**Diminished:** root + minor 3rd + minor 3rd (3 + 3 frets). B diminished = B D F.
Majors sound bright, minors sad, diminished tense, wanting to move on.
minor-dim-chord.summary: Lower the 3rd for minor; lower the 5th too for diminished.
minor-dim-chord.title: Minor and diminished chords

exercises.how: The box most solos start from.
exercises.title: A minor pentatonic, position 1

minor-pent.fix: Your 2021 note says minor pentatonic is the same as major pentatonic minus the 4th and 7th. For minor, drop the 2nd and 6th from the natural minor scale. Your later page gets it right.
steps: Formula: **root, minor 3rd, perfect 4th, perfect 5th, minor 7th**.
A minor pentatonic = **A C D E G**. E minor pentatonic = E G A B D (all in the first 4 frets, starting on open strings).
Movable shape (root on 6th string, fret 5): 6S5F 6S8F · 5S5F 5S7F · 4S5F 4S7F · 3S5F 3S7F · 2S5F 2S8F · 1S5F 1S8F. Use your ring finger to reach the 7th frets.
Exercise: 3 bars of A minor pentatonic, then 1 bar of E minor chord notes, over an A minor backing track.
minor-pent.title: Minor pentatonic

cards.a: W H W W H W W
A B C D E F G

cards.q: Which three notes are lowered compared with major?

steps: Natural minor: **W H W W H W W**.
As intervals: root, major 2nd, **minor 3rd**, perfect 4th, perfect 5th, **minor 6th**, **minor 7th**.
A minor uses the same notes as C major: **A B C D E F G A**. It sounds darker because it centres on A.
Play it in open position, starting and ending on the open A string.
minor-scale.summary: W H W W H W W, starting on A.
minor-scale.title: The natural minor scale

cards.q: Major shape from the 6th string, fret 5, is which key?
Move the major shape to fret 3: which key?

exercises.title: Movable major, A at the 5th fret
Movable minor, A at the 5th fret

steps: **Thumb behind the neck, claw-shaped fingers**, middle finger on the root.
**Major (root on 6th string, going right):** 6S5F 6S7F · 5S4F 5S5F 5S7F · 4S4F 4S6F 4S7F · 3S4F 3S6F 3S7F · 2S5F 2S7F · 1S4F 1S5F. From fret 5 that's A major.
**Minor (root on 6th string):** 6S5F 6S7F 6S8F · 5S5F 5S7F 5S8F · 4S5F 4S7F · 3S4F 3S5F 3S7F · 2S5F 2S6F 2S8F · 1S5F 1S7F 1S8F. From fret 5 that's A minor.
Slide the whole shape to change key: start at fret 8 and the major shape is C major.
movable-scales.summary: 6th-string root shapes you can slide anywhere.
movable-scales.title: Movable major and minor scales

exercises.how: Say each note name out loud.
exercises.title: Natural notes on the 6th string

steps: On the **6th string**: open E, 1 F, 3 G, 5 A, 7 B, 8 C, 10 D, 12 E.
On the **5th string**: open A, 2 B, 3 C, 5 D, 7 E, 8 F, 10 G, 12 A.
The 12th fret is the same note as the open string, one octave up. The fret markers (3, 5, 7, 9, 12) help you find your place.
Test yourself: name a random fret on either string in under two seconds.
natural-notes.summary: Learn these by heart: every barre chord and scale shape starts here.
natural-notes.title: Note names on the 6th and 5th strings

cards.q: Position 5 is the same as which frets an octave down?

steps: Position 1: frets 5–8. Position 2: 7–10. Position 3: 9–13. Position 4: 12–15. Position 5: 14–17 (same as 2–5, an octave down).
Each position shares notes with the next, so you can slide between them.
Your worksheet marks the root A in each box. Find it first, then play the box up and down.
Practise one position per day at a tempo you can play cleanly 3 times.
pent-positions.summary: Connect the boxes across the whole neck.
pent-positions.title: A minor pentatonic: all 5 positions

cards.a: The same phrase with a small change

steps: Create a **phrase**, then 3–4 **variations**: the same idea with a small change.
Go back to the start of the backing track and repeat with a new phrase.
Try the same phrase with different rhythms.
Keep a phrase the same every time you play it. That's what makes it sound intentional.
Over C major, land on G major chord notes in the last bar. Over A minor, land on E minor.
phrase-variation.summary: Make a phrase, then change it a little.
phrase-variation.title: Phrase and variation

cards.q: How many beats in a 4-bar phrase?
Notes of an F major chord?
Notes of a G major chord?

steps: **4 bars = 1 phrase** (16 beats). Most songs are built from phrases.

Exercise: one chord per bar, play its notes across the strings in that bar.
Bar 1 C (C E G) · Bar 2 Am (A C E) · Bar 3 F (F A C) · Bar 4 G (G B D)
Second version: C (C E G) · Dm (D F A) · Em (E G B) · G (G B D).
On beat 1 play the root, on beats 2–4 play the other chord notes.
phrasing.title: Phrasing: four bars

cards.q: Is a power chord major or minor?

steps: A power chord is just **root + 5th** (often + octave). No 3rd, so it's neither major nor minor.
Shape: root on the 6th or 5th string, 5th two frets up on the next string (and octave on the string after).
Livin' on a Prayer moves one shape around: from an A♯ power chord, **+2 frets = C5, +4 = D5, +6 = E5**. Move the same shape.
Mute the other strings with the side of your fretting fingers.
power-chords.summary: Root + 5th: one shape, anywhere on the neck.
power-chords.title: Power chords

cards.q: vi IV V I in C?

cards.a: No, it loops until you land on I
cards.q: Does I IV I V resolve?

steps: **I** is the most important chord, **V** the second. Playing **V → I** at the end sounds resolved.
**IV → I** also resolves, but more gently.
**vi IV V I** (in C: Am F G C) is used in many songs. It moves a lot before it lands.
**I IV I V** doesn't resolve unless it ends on I. It loops and wants to keep going.
In minor keys, i iv v i and VI iv v i do the same job.
progressions.summary: Why V → I sounds like coming home.
progressions.title: Chord function and progressions

steps: The **6th note** of a major scale is the root of its **relative minor**: C major → A minor, G major → E minor.
Same 7 notes, same 7 chords. The difference is which chord feels like home.
If a progression ends on the I chord it sounds major; if it ends on the vi it sounds minor.
Shortcut on the fretboard: from the major root, go down 3 frets.
relative-minor.summary: Every major key shares its notes with a minor key.
relative-minor.title: Relative minor

steps: Write out the song's chords. Find the chord that feels like home (often the first or last).
Check that most chords fit that key's 7 chords, and look for V → I.

Some examples: Zombie → E minor · Perfect → A♭ major · Summer of 69 → D · There She Goes → D · I Love Rock N Roll → A · Zephyr → D · Wonderful Tonight → G · Love Yourself → E · Let It Be → C · Highway to Hell → A.
Californication: its chords (Am F C G Dm) fit both C major and its relative minor, A minor. The song keeps coming home to Am, so it feels like A minor.
song-keys.summary: List its chords, find the home chord and the V.
song-keys.title: Finding the key of a song

cards.a: A B C♯ D E F♯ G♯
A♭ B♭ C D♭ E♭ F G
Each letter is used once, and C is already used
cards.q: Why is A♭ major spelled with D♭, not C♯?

steps: Write the 7 letters from your root, each letter once: e.g. A B C D E F G.
Walk the formula W W H W W W H and add ♯ or ♭ so each step is the right size.
**A major:** A B C♯ D E F♯ G♯ A (3 sharps).
**A♭ major:** A♭ B♭ C D♭ E♭ F G A♭ (4 flats). Use flats here, not sharps, so each letter appears once.
Check with the scale builder below once you've done it on paper.
spell-keys.summary: Use W W H W W W H from any root, one letter each.
spell-keys.title: Spelling any major key

cards.a: E A D G B E
cards.q: What are the string names from 6th to 1st?

cards.a: The 3rd (G) string: its 4th fret matches the open B
cards.q: Which string is tuned at the 4th fret instead of the 5th?
In first position, which finger plays the 3rd fret?

exercises.how: One note per click. Keep each finger over its own fret.
exercises.title: First position, frets 0–4

steps: The six strings, from the thickest (**6th**) to the thinnest (**1st**): **E A D G B E**. The 6th string is the one closest to your face.

**Tune by the 5th fret.** Each string, pressed at the 5th fret, sounds the same as the next open string:
6th string 5th fret = 5th string open
5th string 5th fret = 4th string open
4th string 5th fret = 3rd string open
**3rd string 4th fret** = 2nd string open (the one exception)
2nd string 5th fret = 1st string open
**First position** means your hand covers frets 1–4, one finger per fret: index on 1, middle on 2, ring on 3, little finger on 4.
Play every fret from open to 4 on each string, low E to high e, then back. Say the note names as you go.
strings-tuning.summary: String names, tuning by the 5th fret, one finger per fret.
strings-tuning.title: Strings, tuning and first position

barre.name: Barre chords
steps: For F: lay the index barre first, then add the other fingers one at a time.
Roll the index slightly onto its bony side; that's where it presses best.
Strum, then pick each string to find the one that buzzes.
barre.summary: Place one finger at a time, starting with the corner.

bends.name: Bends
steps: Use three fingers on the string for support. Thumb over the top of the neck.
Rotate your wrist (clockwise for the 2nd/3rd string) and push with your thumb against the neck. The fingers mostly hold.
Bend to pitch: play the target (e.g. 2 frets up) first, then bend until you match it.
Variations you will meet in songs: quick bend, slow bend, bend & release, pre-bend (bend before picking), and bend-and-hold while picking another string.
bends.summary: Push the string to raise the pitch to a target note.
tips: The bent note matches the target exactly

curl.name: Curls (quarter bends)
steps: Bend just a little, about a quarter tone, then let it fall back.
Tabs often mark these as “curl”, sometimes “curl downward”. Used everywhere from Highway to Hell to Sultans of Swing.
curl.summary: A tiny bend for a bluesy, slightly sharp note.

double-stops.name: Double stops ('together')
steps: Tabs often write these as “together”, e.g. 3S7F and 2S8F together.
Barre with one finger if they're on the same fret, or use two fingers.
Add a curl to both at once for the classic rock sound.
double-stops.summary: Two notes at once, often with a curl.

fingerstyle.name: Fingerstyle basics
steps: Thumb plays the root on the 6th, 5th or 4th string (C=5th, G=6th, D=4th).
Index, middle, ring play strings 3, 2, 1.
A common pattern: 6-3-2-1-2-3, and 6-3-2-1-2-3 repeated per chord (Nothing Else Matters, Hallelujah).
Keep the thumb ahead of the fingers so they don't collide.
fingerstyle.summary: Thumb on the bass, fingers 1-2-3 on the top strings.

fretting.name: Clean fretting
steps: Press just behind the fret wire, on the fingertip edge.
Thumb behind the neck, roughly behind your middle finger.
One finger per fret in a position: 1st finger on the 1st fret of the position, 2nd on the 2nd and so on.
fretting.summary: Close to the fret, on the fingertips, thumb behind the neck.

harmonics.name: Harmonics
steps: Lightly touch the string directly over the 12th (or 7th/5th) fret wire, pick, then lift off.
Matilda: touch slightly over the fret line. Nothing Else Matters: 12th-fret harmonics on the open strings.
harmonics.summary: Touch, don't press, right over the fret wire.

hybrid-picking.name: Hybrid picking
steps: Hold the pick normally and pluck higher strings with your middle and ring fingers.
Lets you play two non-adjacent strings at once, as in the double stops in Mary Had a Little Lamb's solo.

legato.name: Hammer-ons and pull-offs
steps: Hammer-on (h): pick, then bring a finger down firmly on a higher fret.
Pull-off (p): pick the higher note and pull the finger off sideways so it plucks the lower note.
2-finger and 3-finger patterns; keep the lower finger planted.
legato.summary: Notes from the fretting hand alone.

muted-strum.name: Muted strums
steps: Keep your fretting fingers on the strings but release the pressure. Then strum: you get a muted 'chk'.
Use it between chords: D (mute) U (mute), as in Another Brick in the Wall and Sultans of Swing.
For a quick mute right after a chord, release the pressure the instant you strum.
muted-strum.summary: Loosen the fretting hand to get the percussive 'chk'.
tips: No notes ringing through the mute

muting.name: Muting unused strings
steps: Picking hand: playing from string 6 to 1, let your palm gradually mute each string you've passed, so only the current string rings.
Fretting hand: going from low strings to high, your index finger naturally mutes the strings below as you move up.
During bends (e.g. 4th string 5th fret to 6th), keep the 5th and 6th strings palm-muted so they don't ring.
muting.summary: Stop strings ringing that you aren't playing.

palm-mute.name: Palm muting
steps: Rest the side of your picking palm lightly where the strings meet the bridge.
Too far forward and the note dies; too far back and it rings fully. Find the chug in between.
Sweet Home Alabama is a great song for practising palm muting; Livin' on a Prayer's intro riff is palm muted too.
palm-mute.summary: Side of the picking hand on the strings by the bridge.
tips: Notes still have pitch, just short and thick

pick-grip.name: Pick grip and alternate picking
steps: Hold the pick between thumb and index finger with three fingers touching; keep your forearm in a straight line with the pick.
Alternate: down on the beat, up on the &. Never two downs in a row on single notes.
Exercise: pick across from the D string to the G string and back, keeping the down-up order.
pick-grip.summary: Relaxed grip, forearm in line, down-up picking.
tips: Small motions: the pick barely leaves the strings

power-chord.name: Power chords
steps: Root with the index, 5th with the ring finger (and octave with the little finger).
Keep your thumb up over the neck for stability.
Mute the strings you aren't playing with the underside of the index.
power-chord.summary: Two or three notes, the rest muted.

practice-deep.name: Practice Deep
steps: Practise slowly, in small batches.
When you make a mistake, restart from the top of the section.
Stop before you're tired and continue tomorrow.
Spend 25% on new material and 75% on review (your 2022 note says 80/20).
tips: Speed comes from clean repetitions, not from playing fast

rake.name: Rakes
steps: Mute the 2–3 strings above your target, then drag the pick across them in one motion so they click before the note.
In Comfortably Numb it's almost like a muted strum but you can hear each note.
rake.summary: Drag the pick across muted strings into the note.

slides.name: Slides
steps: Pick, then slide to the target keeping the same pressure.
Slide from nowhere: start a few frets away without picking a clear note and slide into the target.
Slide to nowhere: after the note, slide away and let it fade (“left” or “right” says which direction).
slides.summary: Glide without lifting; including from and to 'nowhere'.

strumming.name: Strumming patterns
steps: Strum from the wrist, not the elbow. Keep it loose.
Common patterns: D U D U D U · D D · D U D – U D.
Four strums per chord across four chords to start, then mix patterns.
tips: Steady hand motion even when you skip a strum

trill.name: Trills
steps: Pick once, then hammer and pull repeatedly and quickly, as fast as stays even.
Cocaine uses one from an open string.

vibrato.name: Vibrato
steps: 1st: index finger only.
2nd: index and middle together.
3rd: all three fingers for support, in bend position.
Go up, go down, and then both. Keep the speed even.
Then: bend and add vibrato at the top. Hold the pressure while you shake it.
vibrato.summary: Your exercise page: three finger levels, up and down.
tips: Pitch returns to the note each time

whammy.name: Whammy (tremolo) bar
steps: Press the bar down slightly after picking, then release. Small, controlled moves.
Bad Name's solo and Sweet Home Alabama both use it.
whammy.summary: Press and release for dives and wobbles.

a-minor-pent.how: Position 1, frets 5–8: A C D E G. Low E to high e and back. Same notes as C major pentatonic, different home. Say each note name.
a-minor-pent.name: A minor pentatonic, up and down

c-major-pent.how: Same box as A minor pentatonic (frets 5–8), but start and end on C: begin on the low E string, 8th fret, climb to the C on the high e, 8th fret, and come back down to where you started. Say each note: C D E G A C D E G A C.
c-major-pent.name: C major pentatonic, up and down

chromatic.how: One finger per fret. Start on the thick low E string at frets 1–4: index → middle → ring → pinky, alternate picking, then move down string by string to the thin high e. Shift up one fret (2–5) and come back the other way, starting with the pinky: on the high e play A, G♯, G, F♯ (frets 5→2), then the B string E, D♯, D, C♯, and so on up to the low E. Shift up again and repeat. Say each note as you play it.
chromatic.name: Spider crawl, 1-2-3-4

rot-major.how: The key changes every day. Start on the root on the 6th (low E) string, climb across to the root on the 1st (high e) string, then come back down to the root you started on. The root rings twice each time you change direction: the top root at the turnaround, and the bottom root when you go round again. Let each note ring and say each note name.
rot-major.name: Major pentatonic of the day, up and down

rot-minor.how: The relative minor of today's major key: the same five notes, but home is the 6th note of the major scale. Start on that root on the 6th (low E) string, climb to the root on the 1st (high e) string, then come back down to where you started. The root rings twice each time you change direction. Let each note ring and say each note name.
rot-minor.name: Its relative minor pentatonic, up and down

example-12-bar-blues.title: 12-bar blues shuffle in A
example-12-bar-blues.intro: A starter song to show how songs work in Do Not Fret. Learn the shuffle riff first: it's the whole song, moved to three strings. The chord chart shows the 12-bar order, and the lick is a first taste of the A minor pentatonic box.
tips: Keep the riff to two strings and mute the rest with your fretting hand.
Count the 12 bars out loud the first few times.
Play the lick only over the last two bars at first.

sections.name: Shuffle riff on A
sections.teach: Rest your 1st finger on fret 2 of the D string and reach to fret 4 with your 3rd finger. Pick both strings together, slowly, then swing it.

sections.name: Same riff on D
sections.teach: The same shape, one string higher.

sections.name: Same riff on E
sections.teach: The same shape, one string lower.

sections.name: The 12 bars
sections.teach: Play the riff that matches each chord. Bars 9–12 are the turnaround that leads back to the start.

sections.name: Ending lick
sections.teach: A minor pentatonic at the 5th fret, coming down. Learn it without the bend first.

example-ode-to-joy.title: Ode to Joy (melody)
example-ode-to-joy.intro: A first melody, all in open position. Two lines that only differ at the end, so you really only learn one and a half.

sections.name: Line 1
sections.teach: Fingers 2 and 3 for frets 2 and 3. Say the notes: E E F G, G F E D, C C D E, E D D.

sections.name: Line 2
sections.teach: Identical to line 1 until the last bar, which ends on C instead of D.
